findings.title: runSplitQuery interpolates queries twice when called from shard splitting, causing double interpolation of variables
findings.body: runSplitQuery() now maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() at line 296-299. However, runShardSplitQuery() in shardQuerySplitting.ts already interpolates all targets via applyTemplateVariables() at line 49-52 before calling runSplitQuery() (line 163). This means when shard splitting is enabled, every query is interpolated twice. For most variables this is idempotent, but for variables whose interpolated output itself contains variable-like syntax (e.g. a variable value containing '$__rate_interval', or a multi-value variable formatted with a regex/glob that produces '$'-prefixed text), the second pass will re-interpolate and corrupt the query. It also doubles the cost of template variable resolution (which can involve async variable lookups in some datasource implementations) and breaks the invariant that interpolation happens exactly once per query. The fix is to remove the interpolation from runSplitQuery() (or make runShardSplitQuery pass un-interpolated targets), keeping interpolation at exactly one layer — the entry point of the splitting pipeline.

findings.title: runSplitQuery mutates the caller's request object and interpolated targets are shared by reference with sub-requests
findings.body: runSplitQuery() calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, ...) on each target of request.targets. Depending on the datasource implementation, applyTemplateVariables may mutate the query object in place (the shardQuerySplitting test mock at shardQuerySplitting.test.ts:56-59 does exactly this: `query.expr = query.expr.replace(...)`). Since request.targets objects are passed by reference, this mutates the original request the caller (e.g. the datasource query() pipeline or Explore) holds. Additionally, at line 303 `request.queryGroupId = uuidv4()` mutates the caller's request object, and at lines 315/337/344 the code spreads `{ ...request, targets }` — the targets arrays contain the same query object references, so later mutations (e.g. adjustTargetsFromResponseState creates new objects, but interpolateShardingSelector in the shard path mutates expr) can leak across sub-requests. The consequence is that a query issued once can have its expr permanently rewritten (e.g. '$__auto' replaced with '5m'), so a subsequent refresh of the same panel would interpolate an already-interpolated query, producing wrong results or double-interpolation artifacts. The function should clone targets before interpolation (e.g. `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables({ ...query }, ...))`) and avoid mutating the passed-in request.

findings.title: Switch from interpolateVariablesInQueries to applyTemplateVariables changes the interpolation contract (scopedVars/filters handling and per-query vs per-request semantics)
findings.body: runShardSplitQuery() previously called datasource.interpolateVariablesInQueries(request.targets, request.scopedVars), which is the standard Grafana datasource API that interpolates a batch of queries and returns new query objects. The change replaces it with a per-query call to datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters). Two contract differences matter: (1) applyTemplateVariables receives request.filters, which interpolateVariablesInQueries does not — for Loki this is used for ad-hoc filter interpolation, so behavior changes for queries issued with ad-hoc filters; whether that is intended needs verification, and the previous behavior (no filter interpolation in the shard path) may have been deliberate. (2) applyTemplateVariables is documented to return a new query object, but the Loki implementation and the test mocks mutate and return the same object; combined with the shared references described in the querySplitting.ts finding, this creates cross-request contamination. The PR should either keep using interpolateVariablesInQueries (which handles the batch correctly) or ensure applyTemplateVariables results are cloned. At minimum, the behavioral change around request.filters must be intentional and covered by a test with ad-hoc filters present.

findings.title: querySupportsSplitting checks for $__range on the interpolated expr, but interpolation of $__range happens per split sub-range later, so the guard no longer matches the original intent
findings.body: querySupportsSplitting() (line 282-289) excludes queries containing the $__range variable from time splitting, with the comment that $__range is interpolated on the backend with the split time range and would be incorrect. Previously this check ran on the raw, un-interpolated expr, so a query literally containing '$__range' was detected. Now that runSplitQuery() interpolates targets first (line 296-299), the expr passed to querySupportsSplitting has already had template variables replaced. If the user's query contains '$__range', applyTemplateVariables will typically replace it with a concrete duration (e.g. '1d') based on the full request range — so isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) will no longer find '$__range' and the query will be incorrectly included in time splitting. Each split sub-request would then carry a range duration computed from the full range rather than the sub-range, producing wrong results for exactly the queries this guard was written to protect. The range-variable check must run on the original, un-interpolated expr (i.e. partition before mapping through applyTemplateVariables, or check the raw targets in parallel).

findings.title: New shard-splitting interpolation test does not cover the double-interpolation path between runShardSplitQuery and runSplitQuery
findings.body: The new test 'Interpolates queries before execution' (lines 84-101) creates a datasource whose replace() substitutes $__auto and $step, then asserts the final runQuery expr. However, runShardSplitQuery calls runSplitQuery internally (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163), and runSplitQuery now also calls applyTemplateVariables. The test's mock datasource is created via createLokiDatasource({ replace, getVariables }) — if applyTemplateVariables on that mock delegates to replace(), the query is interpolated twice in this test, but the assertions only check the final string, which happens to be stable under double replacement ('5m' contains no variables). There is no test asserting that applyTemplateVariables is called exactly once per query across the shard+split pipeline, and no test with a variable whose value itself contains a variable-like token, which would expose the double-interpolation bug. A test should assert the call count of applyTemplateVariables (or use a non-idempotent replacement) to lock in single interpolation.

findings.title: New interpolation test does not verify that hidden/empty queries are filtered before interpolation, nor that interpolation errors are handled
findings.body: The new test 'Interpolates queries before execution' (lines 75-88) only covers the happy path for a single visible, non-empty query. The interpolation was inserted after the .filter() calls, which is correct, but there is no test confirming that hidden or empty queries are not passed to applyTemplateVariables (avoiding unnecessary variable lookups and side effects), and no test for what happens when applyTemplateVariables throws or returns a query with an empty expr after interpolation (e.g. a variable that resolves to an empty string) — such a query would flow into isLogsQuery/partitioning and be sent to Loki as an empty selector. Given the PR's stated goal is to move interpolation to the start of the process, the edge cases of that reordering (interpolation exceptions aborting the whole split pipeline, empty post-interpolation exprs) should be covered.
